sections.title: Sample
sections.question: Which CEO departures are studied, how many have usable stock returns, and what were the firms like before?
sections.interpretation: The sample holds 1,503 departures with returns: 535 forced exits and 968 voluntary retirements. Firms that fire their CEO are smaller and less profitable the year before: median ROA 7.7% against 12.3% (p <0.001).

methodology.data: Gentry et al. (2021) CEO dismissal database v10Oct2024 linked to daily prices and as-reported annual statements by SEC CIK
methodology.caveat: Founder status and reasons are coded from filings, press releases and news, then checked against the sources.

sections.title: Announcement returns
sections.question: How does the stock react when the board fires the CEO, and does it matter who and why?
sections.interpretation: Over trading days -1 to +1, forced exits earn -2.3% (t = -5.23, N = 532) and retirements -0.3%. Fired founders earn -3.3% against -2.2% (gap p 0.555). Firings over a personal scandal earn -2.5%, other firings -2.3% (gap p 0.836). Prices fall -5.4% over days -30 to -2 and are flat over days +2 to +60 (-1.3%).

methodology.test: Cross-sectional t, Boehmer-Musumeci-Poulsen standardized t, Wilcoxon signed-rank; Welch t and Mann-Whitney U for differences
methodology.data: Daily total returns; market model estimated over trading days -250 to -30 for days -1 to +1; market-adjusted returns for longer windows
methodology.caveat: Day 0 is the first trading day on or after the announcement that the CEO is leaving. Firings for fraud or crime are not in the sample. Reasons other than the checked conduct labels are model codes.

sections.title: Long-run returns
sections.question: Does the firm do better or worse in the 12, 36 and 60 months after the firing?
sections.interpretation: Against the market, the median forced-exit firm returns -5.9% over 12 months, -15.3% over 36 and -31.4% over 60. Against a matched firm the medians are -4.8%, 0.0% and -4.7%.

methodology.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank; skewness-adjusted t with bootstrap CI (Lyon, Barber and Tsai 1999)
methodology.data: Buy-and-hold returns from day +2, delisting returns per Shumway (1997), matched control per Barber and Lyon (1996)
methodology.caveat: Market-adjusted BHARs are skewed and negative for the typical stock; matched-firm BHARs are the main test.

tables.title: Table IA.20. Long-run returns at 12, 36 and 60 months
rows: Panel A. Median return minus the market
Panel B. Median return minus a matched firm
tables.notes: Medians of buy-and-hold returns from day +2 over 12, 36 and 60 months, all firings, with the Wilcoxon p. Panel A subtracts the market's buy-and-hold return; Panel B subtracts a matched firm in the same industry, with market value within 30 percent and the nearest return on assets. The last row gives means with t-test p; skewed returns can give means and medians of opposite sign. Delisted firms take their delisting return and then hold the market. N, 36m counts events at 36 months.

tables.title: Table IA.19. Calendar-time alpha after the announcement
rows: Fired over a personal scandal, 36 months
tables.notes: Each calendar month the portfolio holds every firm whose announcement fell 1 to H months before. Its return minus the risk-free rate is regressed on the Fama-French five factors and momentum; alpha is the intercept, with Newey-West t (6 lags). Value weights are market values at the fiscal year-end before the event. Months with fewer than 10 firms are dropped. The difference rows regress the firing portfolio's return minus the retirement portfolio's. Delisted firms take their delisting return in their last month.

sections.title: Operating performance
sections.question: Does profitability recover after the firing?
sections.interpretation: Against its matched firm, the median forced-exit firm's ROA changes by -0.4 percentage points in fiscal year +1 (p 0.137) and 0.3 in year +3 (p 0.573).

methodology.data: As-reported annual statements; EBITDA over total assets, winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles

tables.title: Table IA.21. Profitability against the matched firm, fiscal years 0 to +3
tables.notes: Median change in return on assets (ROA) from fiscal year -1 to year 0 (the year of the departure), +1, +2 and +3, minus the same change at the matched firm, in percentage points, with the Wilcoxon p in parentheses. ROA is earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) over total assets, winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles. N falls with the horizon because firms stop filing after a sale or bankruptcy.

sections.title: What happened to the firm
sections.question: How often does the firm stop trading within 12, 36 and 60 months, and why?
sections.interpretation: Within 12, 36 and 60 months, 7.6%, 21.5% and 32.1% of forced-exit firms stop trading, against 3.5%, 9.5% and 16.7% after retirements (60-month p <0.001).

tables.notes: Firing effect with controls: the coefficient on the firing dummy in a linear probability model with log market value, return on assets (ROA) in fiscal year -1, event-year and Fama-French industry effects, standard errors clustered by year. The matched row compares each firing firm with its own matched firm (paired t). The rows marked same controls add the prior 12-month return, leverage, book-to-market, an Altman Z distress flag and a loss flag, on the firms with every item; the founder and personal-scandal rows estimate that model within firings. Evidence agreeing or unclear: firings as the evidence-based coding reads them, against retirements. Hazard ratios: Cox model, every month of follow-up to 60 months, industry strata; above one, firing firms leave sooner.

sections.title: Growth after the dismissal
sections.question: Does the firm grow more slowly than its competitor after a founder or scandal dismissal?
sections.interpretation: Against the matched competitor, the median founder firm's revenue growth changes by 2.0 percentage points a year to year +3 (p 0.750, N = 31) and the median hired-CEO firm's by 0.0 percentage points (N = 636); the difference in medians has p 0.733. After a personal scandal the median change is 0.8 percentage points (N = 25).

methodology.test: Wilcoxon signed-rank, one-sample t, Welch t, Mann-Whitney U, Holm across 14 tests; OLS with controls, clustered by firm
methodology.data: Sharadar SF1 as-reported annual statements, fiscal years -3 to +5 around the dismissal year
methodology.caveat: Difference-in-differences against the closest competitor. Ratios use firms still filing; revenue, asset and market value growth are also reported with bankrupt firms and regulatory delistings at -100%. Employees are not in the data.

sections.title: What an investor earns after the firing
sections.question: From the moment a founder firing is public, does the firm's stock beat or trail the stock market?
sections.interpretation: Bought at the close of the day after the announcement and held 12 months, $100 in the median founder firm is worth $114.67, against $111.90 in the S&P 500 (N = 57).

methodology.test: Skewness-adjusted t and bootstrap on buy-and-hold gaps; Wilcoxon; calendar-time CAPM and five-factor plus momentum alphas with Newey-West errors, Holm across holding periods
methodology.data: Sharadar daily prices and corporate actions; SPY dividend-adjusted close; Kenneth French factors
methodology.caveat: Founder firings are few, so the calendar-time portfolio holds few firms in most months; the number held is reported.

statistics.label: fwd.forced.d0.ind.m1.beat share
statistics.test: binomial test of a share of one half
statistics.population: CEOs fired for any reason but fraud or other legal violation, against the industry average; S&P 1500 firms, announcements 1998-2023

sections.title: When the market prices the news
sections.question: How much of the reaction to a dismissal comes at the first trade, and does anything remain for an investor after it?
sections.interpretation: For all dismissals the overnight gap on the first tradeable day is -1.0%; for founders the five-day short from the open earns 5.4% (Holm p 0.114).

methodology.test: Skewness-adjusted and firm-clustered t; Wilcoxon; Holm within group; calendar-time alphas with Newey-West errors
methodology.data: Sharadar daily open and close; SPY; EDGAR 8-K acceptance times; Alpha Vantage 1-minute bars; Kenneth French daily factors
methodology.caveat: The 8-K acceptance time is an upper bound on the release time; about 40% of dismissals cannot be timed.

tables.title: Table IA.33. When the market prices the news: the first tradeable day against the long horizon
rows: Panel A. Return minus the S&P 500, by window
First tradeable day, overnight gap, mean
First tradeable day, open to close, mean
First tradeable day, close to close, mean
First tradeable day, close to close, median
Panel B. Release time and the overnight gap
Overnight gap, released before the open, mean
Overnight gap, released after the close, mean
Days +2 to +5, release time unknown, mean
Panel C. Short the firm, hold the S&P 500, release time known (p Holm-adjusted)
From the open, 5 days, net of 50 bp
Panel D. Calendar-time six-factor alpha, held from the close of the first tradeable day
tables.notes: Well-dated dismissals for any reason but fraud. Release time: when the firm's 8-K was accepted by EDGAR, New York time, the latest the news could have been public. First tradeable day: the announcement day for releases before the close, else the next day. Returns are the firm's minus the S&P 500's with dividends. p: skewness-adjusted t (Panels A and B), Holm-adjusted across each group's eight rules (Panel C), Newey-West (Panel D). Panel C uses only releases with a known time; a positive return is a gain to the short seller, before borrowing costs. Panel D: daily intercept of an equal-weighted portfolio on five Fama-French factors and momentum; N counts trading days.
